picks.title: Melancholy
picks.creator: Edvard Munch
picks.credit: "Melancholy" by Edvard Munch, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Edvard_Munch_-_Melancholy_(1894).jpg).
picks.why: A lone figure sits hunched, head in hand, at the lower right while an empty shoreline and still water stretch away to the left. That is the burnout mood exactly: quiet, inward, a little lonely. Borrow the right-weighted figure and the long, low-contrast sweep of shore, which leaves the left half calm enough for a title.

picks.title: Interior with Young Woman Seen from Behind
picks.creator: Vilhelm Hammershøi
picks.credit: "Interior with Young Woman from Behind [ 1 ] or Young Woman from Behind . [ 2 ]" by Vilhelm Hammershøi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vilhelm_Hammershoi_-_Interieur_mit_Rueckenansicht_einer_Frau_-_1903-1904_-_Randers_Kunstmuseum.jpg).
picks.why: A woman seen from behind in a bare grey interior: no face, no event, just stillness and isolation. The muted palette and expanses of plain wall give a quiet, slightly lonely atmosphere and flat areas where type can sit. Borrow the turned-away figure and the desaturated grey-white tonality.

X.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons). Crop so the figure sits right of the title area.

picks.title: Interior with Young Woman Seen from Behind
picks.creator: Vilhelm Hammershøi
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: Vilhelm Hammershøi, Interior with Young Woman Seen from Behind, 1903–04, Randers Kunstmuseum. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A lone woman in black stands with her back to us on the right, facing a bare grey wall; the left half is almost empty wall, an ideal quiet field for the title. Borrow the muted grey palette, the turned-away figure (isolation without melodrama) and the generous negative space.

picks.title: The Monk by the Sea
picks.creator: Caspar David Friedrich
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: Caspar David Friedrich, The Monk by the Sea, 1808–10, Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: One tiny figure against an enormous empty sky and dark sea: the classic image of smallness and solitude. About four-fifths of the canvas is sky, so a title fits in the upper left; the low horizon and desaturated tones carry exhaustion quietly.

picks.title: Singing Angels (Ghent Altarpiece, detail)
picks.creator: Jan van Eyck / Hubert van Eyck
picks.credit: "Dutch: Zingende engelen Singing Angels" by Jan van Eyck / Hubert van Eyck, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jan_van_Eyck_-_The_Ghent_Altarpiece_-_Singing_Angels_(detail)_-_WGA07642.jpg).
picks.why: A tightly packed group of singers, mouths open and faces overlapping, all singing from one lectern: the most literal image of many voices together. The gold, brocade and warm reds give warmth and a church setting at once. Borrow the dense cluster of faces as one mass, cropped close.

picks.title: Choir singing during Easter service at Corpus Christi Church
picks.creator: Marjory Collins
picks.credit: "Choir singing during Easter service at Corpus Christi Church8d16975v" by Marjory Collins, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Choir_singing_during_Easter_service_at_Corpus_Christi_Church8d16975v.jpg).
picks.why: A real parish choir singing during an Easter service, documentary rather than idealised, so it reads as community rather than performance. Borrow the rows of ordinary people side by side in a church interior; warm the colour for the poster.

X.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons; the second is a 1943 US Office of War Information photograph from the Library of Congress).

picks.title: A Village Choir
picks.creator: Thomas Webster
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: Thomas Webster, A Village Choir, 1847, Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A crowded church gallery of ordinary villagers singing and playing together, in a warm brown and amber palette. It shows exactly the community-choir-in-a-church idea; borrow the packed, overlapping faces and the warm candle-wood tones for a poster that feels homely, not formal.

picks.title: Watoto Church Choir singing during the 33rd Coronation anniversary
picks.creator: Namwanje Sauyah
picks.credit: Photo: Namwanje Sauyah, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A dense row of singers in bright, warm clothing, mouths open mid-song, with faces repeating into the depth of the frame: 'lots of voices together' made visible. It is a church choir but photographed at a civic event, not inside a church, so use it for the crowd rhythm and warmth. Identifiable people: CC0 covers copyright, not personality rights, so check before using it in advertising.

picks.title: Searchlights on the Rock of Gibraltar, 1942
picks.creator: Dallison G W (Lieut), War Office official photographer
picks.credit: "Searchlights on the Rock of Gibraltar, 1942" by Dallison G W (Lieut), War Office official photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Searchlights_on_the_Rock_of_Gibraltar,_1942.jpg).
picks.why: Searchlight beams sweep a night sky from a fortified rock: vigilance and defence made visible, tense but controlled, with nothing of hoodies or green code. Borrow the dark field cut by crossing beams as a metaphor for scanning and monitoring.

picks.title: The Little Owl
picks.creator: Albrecht Dürer
picks.credit: "The Little Owl" by Albrecht Dürer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Albrecht_D%C3%BCrer_-_The_Little_Owl_-_WGA7367.jpg).
picks.why: A small owl stares straight at the viewer with wide, alert eyes: watchful, attentive, slightly unsettling, a guardian that sees in the dark without any tech cliche. Borrow the direct frontal gaze and the isolated subject on a plain ground, which leaves headline space.

X.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons). The 1942 photograph is a British War Office official photograph listed as public domain on Commons.

picks.title: Seeing stars (SEST telescope at La Silla)
picks.creator: Sangku Kim / ESO
picks.credit: Sangku Kim/ESO, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A big dish stands alone under a dark star field, attentive and still. It reads as 'listening and watching' without screens, code or hoodies. Borrow the dark-blue night, the single sensor turned toward the unknown, and the tension of a small lit structure against vast darkness.

picks.title: The IRAM 30-meter telescope scanning the night sky
picks.creator: IRAM-gre (IRAM)
picks.credit: IRAM-gre, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A radio telescope sweeping the night sky: constant, active vigilance, which is the idea behind security monitoring. Its strong geometric silhouette crops well for a wide hero. Note: CC BY-SA means a modified version (a crop or overlay) must be shared under the same licence, so check that suits the website.

picks.title: Salmon fishing on Columbia River, Ore.: 10 fishermen posed with net and catch
picks.creator: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress
picks.credit: "Salmon fishing on Columbia River, Ore.- 10 fishermen posed with net and catch LCCN2006688449" by Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Salmon_fishing_on_Columbia_River,_Ore.-_10_fishermen_posed_with_net_and_catch_LCCN2006688449.jpg).
picks.why: Fishermen posed with a net and a large haul of salmon on the Columbia River in 1895: documentary evidence of past abundance. Paired with a single fish it makes the then-versus-now scale argument without a chart. Borrow the mass of fish as the 'then' half of the cover.

picks.title: Salmon
picks.creator: Takahashi Yuichi
picks.credit: "Salmon" by Takahashi Yuichi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Salmon_by_Takahashi_Yuichi_(Geidai_Museum).jpg).
picks.why: A single half-cut salmon hangs alone against a plain ground in a tall, narrow format, painted with stark realism. One isolated fish reads as scarcity and loss. Borrow the lone vertical fish and the empty space around it as the 'now' half of the cover.

X.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons; the first via the Library of Congress).

picks.title: Fishermen on beach harvesting salmon catch, vicinity of the lower Columbia River, ca 1900
picks.creator: John Fletcher Ford
picks.date: c. 1900 (University of Washington Libraries, Industries and Occupations Photographs, INDOCC 631)
picks.credit: John Fletcher Ford, c. 1900. University of Washington Libraries Special Collections. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A beach covered in salmon from one seine haul shows historic abundance at a glance. Use it as the 'past' half of a then/now contrast, perhaps faded sepia, against a sparse present-day image. The print's 'Copyrighted' caption dates from c. 1900; that copyright has long expired.

picks.title: Sockeye salmon sun glistening
picks.creator: Lisa Hupp / U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
picks.date: undated (in USFWS 2021 Fish and Aquatic Conservation Annual Report)
picks.licence: Public domain (work of a US federal employee)
picks.credit: Lisa Hupp/USFWS. Public domain.
picks.why: A single red sockeye in clear water: the 'now' half, one fish where there were thousands. Put it small in a lot of empty space, or set it beside the 1900 haul, so the scale gap reads instantly on the cover. Not a US government endorsement; credit USFWS as courtesy.

picks.title: The Brioche
picks.creator: Edouard Manet
picks.credit: Edouard Manet, The Brioche, 1870. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. CC0 (Gift and Bequest of David and Peggy Rockefeller, 1991, 2017).
picks.why: One golden brioche sits on top of the arrangement, crowned with a flower and lit against a dark ground: a single bake as the clear hero of the picture, with a celebratory feel. Borrow the single raised, spotlit bake for the anniversary post.

picks.title: Arranging loaves in Lithuanian bakery, Pittsburgh
picks.creator: Marjory Collins
picks.credit: "Arranging loaves in Lithuanian bakery. Pittsburgh, United States" by Marjory Collins, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Arranging_loaves_in_Lithuanian_bakery_8d19624v.jpg).
picks.why: A baker arranging rows of loaves in a 1943 neighbourhood bakery: the many 'others' the hero loaf stands out from, plus craft and heritage that suit a 20th anniversary. Borrow the repeating rows as the field into which one highlighted loaf is set.

X.note: Both from live searches of public collections (the Met; Wikimedia Commons via the Library of Congress, a 1943 Office of War Information photograph).

picks.title: Domaći hljeb sa sjemenkama u pekari (home-style seeded bread in a bakery)
picks.creator: Minja Klarić
picks.credit: Minja Klarić, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: One dark, seed-crusted loaf stands upright in front of a rack of pale white loaves. It is almost exactly the brief: one loaf distinguished by texture and colour. The vertical framing suits a 4:5 or Story crop. CC BY-SA: edits must stay under CC BY-SA, with credit given.

picks.title: The Baker
picks.creator: Job Adriaensz. Berckheyde
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: Job Berckheyde, The Baker, c. 1681, Worcester Art Museum. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A Haarlem baker blows a horn to announce fresh bread, with loaves on the sill: heritage, craft and celebration together. It works as a mood and layout reference for an anniversary post: a window frame, warm light, and the bread presented like a proud announcement.

picks.title: The Avenue at Middelharnis
picks.creator: Meindert Hobbema
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: Meindert Hobbema, The Avenue at Middelharnis, 1689, National Gallery, London. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: The textbook one-point perspective: a road lined with tall trees runs straight to a vanishing point on a low horizon, under a big sky. Borrow the converging lines that drag the eye forward, and put 'Where we are going' in the open sky.

picks.title: Historic Route 66 near Amboy, California
picks.creator: Dietmar Rabich
picks.credit: Dietmar Rabich / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
picks.why: A straight desert road running to the horizon in a wide panoramic format (about 2:1), so it suits a 16:9 slide. A clean, modern take on the same pull-to-the-horizon idea. CC BY-SA: credit the author; adapted versions must carry the same licence.

picks.title: The Avenue at Middelharnis
picks.creator: Meindert Hobbema
picks.credit: "German: Allee von Middelharnis The Avenue at Middelharnis" by Meindert Hobbema, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hobbema_Het_laantje_van_Middelharnis.jpg).
picks.why: A straight avenue of tall trees runs from the viewer to a vanishing point on a low horizon: classic one-point perspective that pulls the eye forward and away. Borrow the converging road and low horizon as the structure for 'Where we are going', with the title in the open sky.

picks.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
picks.creator: Caspar David Friedrich
picks.credit: "The hiker above the sea of fog" by Caspar David Friedrich, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Wanderer_above_the_sea_of_fog.jpg).
picks.why: A figure seen from behind looks over a sea of fog toward distant peaks, so the viewer looks where he looks. Borrow the back-turned figure as a stand-in for the team and the vast distance ahead; crop wide to keep the horizon dominant.

Y.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons).

picks.title: Moonlight, Wood Island Light
picks.creator: Winslow Homer
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: Winslow Homer, Moonlight, Wood Island Light, 1894, The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Public domain.
picks.why: A night sea crashing on rocks, nearly all dark, with a lighthouse's small point of light in the distance. It suits a literary cover: painterly, menacing, restrained. Borrow the near-black palette and the single distant light as the focal point.

picks.title: Sidi Bou Afi Lighthouse, El Jadida, Morocco
picks.creator: Belbachirkamal
picks.credit: Belbachirkamal, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A lighthouse at night in fog, its beams visible as solid shafts against a dark sky, in portrait orientation like a book cover. Borrow the beam as a graphic element, which can also point to the title. CC BY-SA: the cover design built on it may need to be licensed CC BY-SA, so a commercial publisher may prefer it as a reference only.

picks.title: A Moonlight with a Lighthouse, Coast of Tuscany
picks.creator: Joseph Wright of Derby
picks.credit: "A Moonlight with a Lighthouse, Coast of Tuscany" by Joseph Wright of Derby, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_(1734-1797)_-_A_Moonlight_with_a_Lighthouse,_Coast_of_Tuscany_-_N05882_-_National_Gallery.jpg).
picks.why: A dark coast at night with a lighthouse on a rock: the picture is mostly deep shadow, with moonlight and the lighthouse giving the only strong light. Borrow the near-black field and the single bright point, leaving dark space for the title.

picks.title: Bell Rock Lighthouse during a storm from the northeast
picks.creator: After J. M. W. Turner
picks.credit: "Bell Rock Lighthouse during a storm from the northeast." by After J. M. W. Turner, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bell_Rock_Lighthouse_during_a_storm_cph.3b18344.jpg).
picks.why: A lone lighthouse besieged by enormous waves: menace and isolation, the setting of a thriller. It is lighter than the brief asks, so take the drama of the small tower against overwhelming water and darken it heavily.

Y.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons; the second is a print after Turner from the Library of Congress).

picks.title: Nocturne: Blue and Silver – Chelsea
picks.creator: James McNeill Whistler
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Silver – Chelsea, 1871, Tate. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: Almost a single field of soft blue-green with a low horizon, a few faint lights and one small boat. It is the calmest image I know, and easy to crop wide. Borrow the one-hue palette, the misty edges and the near-absence of detail for a sleep banner with text overlaid.

picks.title: Moonlight, Strandgade 30
picks.creator: Vilhelm Hammershøi
picks.licence: CC0 (The Met Open Access; public-domain painting)
picks.credit: Vilhelm Hammershøi, Moonlight, Strandgade 30, 1900–06, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access, CC0).
picks.why: An empty room at night, with soft moonlight from a window falling on the wall and floor. It feels hushed and domestic, like a bedroom just before sleep. Borrow the low-contrast greys, the single soft light source, and the absence of anything busy.

picks.title: Nocturne: Blue and Silver - Chelsea
picks.creator: James McNeill Whistler
picks.credit: "Nocturne: Blue and Silver - Chelsea" by James McNeill Whistler, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler_-_Nocturne-_Blue_and_Silver_-_Chelsea_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).
picks.why: A river at dusk reduced to soft blue-grey bands, a few faint lights and one small boat: almost nothing happens, which is the point. Borrow the near-monochrome blue palette, the broad horizontal bands and the low detail for a wide, calm sleep banner.

picks.title: The Calm Sea
picks.creator: Gustave Courbet
picks.credit: Gustave Courbet, The Calm Sea, 1869. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. CC0 (H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929).
picks.why: A flat calm sea under a vast soft sky with only a couple of boats on the shore: wide, quiet and uncluttered. Borrow the long horizontal format, low horizon and gentle tonal gradients so interface text can sit on the sky.

Y.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons; the Met).

picks.title: Meeting of Waters (Manaus)
picks.creator: Ana Claudia Jatahy – MTUR (Brazilian Ministry of Tourism)
picks.licence: CC0 (as tagged on Commons, from the Ministry of Tourism Flickr)
picks.credit: Ana Claudia Jatahy / MTUR, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: The dark Rio Negro and the sandy Solimões run side by side as one river without mixing at first: two departments that are clearly different but now share one channel. Borrow the clean two-tone split for the slide, with each half labelled.

picks.title: Confluence de l'Arve et du Rhône (Geneva)
picks.creator: Christian David
picks.credit: Christian David, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: The clear blue Rhône meets the silty grey Arve and they flow on together, with a visible seam between them. It is a European, urban counterpart to the Manaus image, and the high-resolution landscape format suits a slide. Credit the author.

picks.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
picks.creator: Jan van Eyck
picks.credit: "The Arnolfini Portrait label QS:Lde-ch,"Arnolfini-Hochzeit" label QS:Len-gb,"Arnolfini Portrait" label QS:Len-ca,"Arnolfini Portrait" label QS:Lpt-br,"O Casal Arnolfini"" by Jan van Eyck, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Eyck,_Jan_van_-_Arnolfini_Portrait_-_NG.jpg).
picks.why: Two people clearly bound together by joined hands at the centre, yet differently dressed, posed and lit, each with their own side of the room: partnership between distinct parties. Borrow the two-figure composition with the joined hands as the visual hinge of the slide.

picks.title: Shoes
picks.creator: Vincent van Gogh
picks.credit: Vincent van Gogh, Shoes, 1888. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. CC0 (Purchase, The Annenberg Foundation Gift, 1992).
picks.why: A pair of worn shoes: obviously a pair, yet each differs in pose and wear. A simple, unpretentious metaphor for two departments that belong together. Borrow the matched-but-different pair on a plain ground.

Y.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons; the Met).

picks.title: The City Rises
picks.creator: Umberto Boccioni
picks.credit: "The City Rises" by Umberto Boccioni, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Immagine-Umberto_boccioni_la_citt%C3%A0_che_sale.jpg).
picks.why: A huge horse surges forward while workers strain and a city is built around them, all in rushing, swirling brushstrokes: growth and construction as raw energy. Borrow the diagonal thrust and blurred motion for a spread about expanding markets.

picks.title: Rain, Steam and Speed - The Great Western Railway
picks.creator: J. M. W. Turner
picks.credit: "Rain, Steam and Speed - The Great Western Railway ; the painting depicts an early locomotive of the Great Western Railway crossing the River Thames on Brunel's recently completed Maidenhead Railway Bridge .The painting is also credited for allowing a glimpse of the Romantic strife within Turner and " by J. M. W. Turner, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Turner_-_Rain,_Steam_and_Speed_-_National_Gallery_file.jpg).
picks.why: A locomotive charges out of rain and light along a bridge that cuts diagonally across the picture: the classic image of progress and forward movement. Borrow the strong diagonal and the sense of something emerging from haze, which suits 'emerging' markets.

X.note: Both from live searches of public collections (Wikimedia Commons). Boccioni died in 1916, so the painting is public domain.

picks.title: Rain, Steam and Speed – The Great Western Railway
picks.creator: J. M. W. Turner
picks.licence: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons tag; author died 70+ years ago)
picks.credit: J. M. W. Turner, Rain, Steam and Speed – The Great Western Railway, 1844, National Gallery, London. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A locomotive bursts out of golden haze along a diagonal bridge: the classic painting of energy and the new rushing forward. Borrow the strong diagonal, the warm, high-energy palette and the motion blur for a spread about growth, while keeping the reference abstract rather than literally Victorian.

picks.title: Night Light Trail, Maryland, Lagos, Nigeria
picks.creator: Omoeko Media
picks.credit: Omoeko Media, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
picks.why: A long exposure of traffic streaming through Lagos at night: literal forward motion in a fast-growing emerging-market city, which avoids generic stock skylines. Borrow the streaking light lines as a directional graphic motif across the spread. CC BY-SA: adaptations must stay under the same licence; I did not view this image myself.
